titleStmt.title: Prospect Theory: An Analysis of Decision under Risk

Amos Tversky

bibl.title: Prospect Theory: An Analysis of Decision under Risk

person.p: the tag layer; a sentence written by the tagger about the paper, always anchored to a quotation but not itself a quotation

span.label: mechanism
span.quote: The same psychological principle-the overweighting of certainty-favors risk aversion in the domain of gains and risk seeking in the domain of losses.

span.label: decision making under risk
span.quote: The present paper describes several classes of choice problems in which preferences systematically violate the axioms of expected utility theory.

span.label: behavioural-experiment
span.quote: The demonstrations are based on the responses of students and university faculty to hypothetical choice problems.

span.label: mechanisms
span.term: A THEORY'S NORMATIVE AND DESCRIPTIVE USES ARE SEPARATED AND ONLY ONE IS ATTACKED: expected utility theory is GENERALLY ACCEPTED AS A NORMATIVE MODEL of rational choice and WIDELY APPLIED AS A DESCRIPTIVE MODEL of economic behaviour - so it is assumed both that all reasonable people WOULD WISH to obey the axioms and that most people ACTUALLY DO. Two different claims travel under one theory's name
span.quote: EXPECTED UTILITY THEORY has dominated the analysis of decision making under risk. It has been generally accepted as a normative model of rational choice [24], and widely applied as a descriptive model of economic behavior, e.g. [15, 4]. Thus, it is assumed that all reasonable people would wish to obey the axioms of the theory [47, 36], and that most people actually do, most of the time.

span.label: mechanisms
span.term: AND THE TARGET IS THE THEORY AS INTERPRETED AND APPLIED, NOT THE FORMALISM: the paper describes classes of problems in which preferences SYSTEMATICALLY VIOLATE the axioms, and concludes that utility theory AS IT IS COMMONLY INTERPRETED AND APPLIED is not an adequate DESCRIPTIVE model. The qualifier is doing the work - what fails is a use of the theory
span.quote: The present paper describes several classes of choice problems in which preferences systematically violate the axioms of expected utility theory. In the light of these observations we argue that utility theory, as it is commonly interpreted and applied, is not an adequate descriptive model and we propose an alternative account of choice under risk.

span.label: mechanisms
span.term: A PHENOMENON IS NAMED AT THE MOMENT IT IS INTRODUCED, AND THE NAME CARRIES THE MECHANISM: people underweight outcomes that are MERELY PROBABLE compared with outcomes obtained with CERTAINTY, and THIS TENDENCY, CALLED THE CERTAINTY EFFECT, is what contributes to risk aversion for sure gains and risk seeking for sure losses
span.quote: In particular, people underweight outcomes that are merely probable in comparison with outcomes that are obtained with certainty. This tendency, called the certainty effect, contributes to risk aversion in choices involving sure gains and to risk seeking in choices involving sure losses.

span.label: mechanisms
span.term: THE SECOND NAMED TENDENCY IS EXPLICITLY A FACT ABOUT DESCRIPTION: people DISCARD COMPONENTS SHARED BY ALL PROSPECTS under consideration, and THIS TENDENCY, CALLED THE ISOLATION EFFECT, LEADS TO INCONSISTENT PREFERENCES WHEN THE SAME CHOICE IS PRESENTED IN DIFFERENT FORMS. The inconsistency is produced by the form, not by the choice
span.quote: In addition, people generally discard components that are shared by all prospects under consideration. This tendency, called the isolation effect, leads to inconsistent preferences when the same choice is presented in different forms.

span.label: mechanisms
span.term: A FORMAL OPERATIONALISATION IS REPORTED AS FAILING TO CAPTURE THE INTUITIVE NOTION IT STANDS FOR: the aversion to probabilistic insurance is called A RATHER PUZZLING CONSEQUENCE of the risk aversion hypothesis, and the conclusion drawn is that THE INTUITIVE NOTION OF RISK IS NOT ADEQUATELY CAPTURED BY THE ASSUMED CONCAVITY of the utility function for wealth. The formalism and the word have come apart, and the paper says which is at fault
span.quote: This is a rather puzzling consequence of the risk aversion hypothesis of utility theory, because probabilistic insurance appears intuitively riskier than regular insurance, which entirely eliminates the element of risk. Evidently, the intuitive notion of risk is not adequately captured by the assumed concavity of the utility function for wealth.

span.label: mechanisms
span.term: THE CONTRAST CLASS IS DISSOLVED INTO A MATTER OF DEGREE BEFORE ANY NEW TERM IS OFFERED: the aversion to probabilistic insurance is called PARTICULARLY INTRIGUING because ALL INSURANCE IS, IN A SENSE, PROBABILISTIC - even the most avid buyer REMAINS VULNERABLE to many risks his policies do not cover. What looked like two kinds of thing is shown to be one kind at two settings
span.quote: The aversion for probabilistic insurance is particularly intriguing because all insurance is, in a sense, probabilistic. The most avid buyer of insurance remains vulnerable to many financial and other risks which his policies do not cover.

span.label: mechanisms
span.term: THE THESIS IS STATED IN ONE SENTENCE AND THE DEMONSTRATIONS ARE PROMISED: two prospects that are EQUIVALENT IN PROBABILITIES AND OUTCOMES COULD HAVE DIFFERENT VALUES DEPENDING ON THEIR FORMULATION. Everything else in the section is evidence for that one claim about description
span.quote: Thus, two prospects that are equivalent in probabilities and outcomes could have different values depending on their formulation. Several demonstrations of this general phenomenon are described in the next section.

span.label: mechanisms
span.term: THE MECHANISM IS THAT ONE OBJECT ADMITS MORE THAN ONE DECOMPOSITION: to simplify a choice people disregard components the alternatives SHARE and focus on those that DISTINGUISH them - which may produce inconsistent preferences BECAUSE A PAIR OF PROSPECTS CAN BE DECOMPOSED INTO COMMON AND DISTINCTIVE COMPONENTS IN MORE THAN ONE WAY, and different decompositions sometimes lead to different preferences
span.quote: In order to simplify the choice between alternatives, people often disregard components that the alternatives share, and focus on the components that distinguish them (Tversky [44]). This approach to choice problems may produce inconsistent preferences, because a pair of prospects can be decomposed into common and distinctive components in more than one way, and different decompositions sometimes lead to different preferences. We refer to this phenomenon as the isolation effect.

span.label: mechanisms
span.term: THE DIFFERENCE BETWEEN TWO FORMULATIONS IS LOCATED IN THE REPRESENTATION ITSELF: the ESSENTIAL DIFFERENCE between the two decision trees is IN THE LOCATION OF THE DECISION NODE - in the standard form the decision maker faces a choice between two RISKY prospects, and in the sequential form between a RISKY AND A RISKLESS one. The same underlying gamble, two diagrams, and the contrast that drives the effect is a feature of the diagram
span.quote: The essential difference between the two representations is in the location of the decision node. In the standard form (Figure 1), the decision maker faces a choice between two risky prospects, whereas in the sequential form (Figure 2) he faces a choice between a risky and a riskless prospect.

span.label: mechanisms
span.term: THE EFFECT IS PRESENTED AS FALSIFYING A FOUNDATIONAL SUPPOSITION RATHER THAN AS A CURIOSITY: the reversal of preferences due to the dependency among events is PARTICULARLY SIGNIFICANT BECAUSE IT VIOLATES THE BASIC SUPPOSITION of a decision-theoretical analysis, THAT CHOICES BETWEEN PROSPECTS ARE DETERMINED SOLELY BY THE PROBABILITIES OF FINAL STATES
span.quote: The reversal of preferences due to the dependency among events is particularly significant because it violates the basic supposition of a decision-theoretical analysis, that choices between prospects are determined solely by the probabilities of final states.

span.label: mechanisms
span.term: WHICH REPRESENTATION IS NATURAL IS ITSELF A PROPERTY OF THE PROBLEM, NOT A FREE CHOICE: it is EASY TO THINK OF decision problems MOST NATURALLY REPRESENTED in one of the forms rather than the other - a choice between two risky ventures is likely to be viewed in the standard form, and the paper then gives a problem that is MOST LIKELY TO BE REPRESENTED in the sequential form
span.quote: It is easy to think of decision problems that are most naturally represented in one of the forms above rather than in the other. For example, the choice between two different risky ventures is likely to be viewed in the standard form. On the other hand, the following problem is most likely to be represented in the sequential form.

span.label: mechanisms
span.term: THE THEORY PUTS A RE-DESCRIPTION STEP BEFORE THE EVALUATION STEP AND MODELS IT SEPARATELY: two phases are distinguished, an early phase of EDITING and a subsequent phase of EVALUATION, and the function of the editing phase is TO ORGANIZE AND REFORMULATE THE OPTIONS so as to simplify subsequent choice. A formal theory of how a problem is restated before it is answered
span.quote: Prospect theory distinguishes two phases in the choice process: an early phase of editing and a subsequent phase of evaluation. The editing phase consists of a preliminary analysis of the offered prospects, which often yields a simpler representation of these prospects. In the second phase, the edited prospects are evaluated and the prospect of highest value is chosen. We next outline the editing phase, and develop a formal model of the evaluation phase. The function of the editing phase is to organize and reformulate the options so as to simplify subsequent evaluation and choice.

span.label: mechanisms
span.term: THE REFERENCE POINT THAT DECIDES WHAT COUNTS AS A GAIN IS ITSELF SET BY THE FORMULATION: gains and losses are DEFINED RELATIVE TO SOME NEUTRAL REFERENCE POINT, usually the current asset position - but THE LOCATION OF THE REFERENCE POINT, AND THE CONSEQUENT CODING OF OUTCOMES AS GAINS OR LOSSES, CAN BE AFFECTED BY THE FORMULATION of the offered prospects and by the decision maker's expectations
span.quote: Gains and losses, of course, are defined relative to some neutral reference point. The reference point usually corresponds to the current asset position, in which case gains and losses coincide with the actual amounts that are received or paid. However, the location of the reference point, and the consequent coding of outcomes as gains or losses, can be affected by the formulation of the offered prospects, and by the expectations of the decision maker.

span.label: mechanisms
span.term: AND THE CONCLUSION IS STATED AS A PROPERTY OF PREFERENCE ORDERS: MANY ANOMALIES OF PREFERENCE RESULT FROM THE EDITING OF PROSPECTS, and MORE GENERALLY THE PREFERENCE ORDER BETWEEN PROSPECTS NEED NOT BE INVARIANT ACROSS CONTEXTS, BECAUSE THE SAME OFFERED PROSPECT COULD BE EDITED IN DIFFERENT WAYS DEPENDING ON THE CONTEXT IN WHICH IT APPEARS. The order is a property of the description as much as of the object
span.quote: Many anomalies of preference result from the editing of prospects. For example, the inconsistencies associated with the isolation effect result from the cancellation of common components. Some intransitivities of choice are explained by a simplification that eliminates small differences between prospects (see Tversky [43]). More generally, the preference order between prospects need not be invariant across contexts, because the same offered prospect could be edited in different ways depending on the context in which it appears.

span.label: the analysis is restricted to prospects with objective/standard probabilities
span.note: what this limits: the scope of the whole treatment: THE PRESENT DISCUSSION IS RESTRICTED TO PROSPECTS WITH SO-CALLED OBJECTIVE OR STANDARD PROBABILITIES
span.quote: The present discussion is restricted to prospects with so-called objective or standard probabilities.

span.label: The findings rest on hypothetical rather than real choices, which raises validity and generalisability questions the authors acknowledge.
span.note: what this limits: every empirical result in the paper: THE RELIANCE ON HYPOTHETICAL CHOICES RAISES OBVIOUS QUESTIONS REGARDING THE VALIDITY OF THE METHOD AND THE GENERALIZABILITY OF THE RESULTS
span.quote: The reliance on hypothetical choices raises obvious questions regarding the validity of the method and the generalizability of the results.

span.label: The order in which editing operations are applied, and hence the final edited prospect, is not determined by the theory and is left unstudied.
span.note: what this limits: the determinacy of the model's own predictions: the order of editing operations decides the final edited prospect, and A DETAILED STUDY OF THIS PROBLEM IS BEYOND THE SCOPE OF THE PRESENT TREATMENT
span.quote: A detailed study of this problem is beyond the scope of the present treatment.

span.label: The theory's account of insurance and gambling is admittedly incomplete.
span.note: what this limits: the insurance-and-gambling account specifically: WE FEEL THAT THE PRESENT ANALYSIS FALLS FAR SHORT OF A FULLY ADEQUATE ACCOUNT OF THESE COMPLEX PHE[nomena]
span.quote: Although prospect theory predicts both insurance and gambling for small probabilities, we feel that the present analysis falls far short of a fully adequate account of these complex phenomena.

span.label: The treatment covers only the simplest two-prospect choice task, not bidding or other production tasks.
span.note: what this limits: the task the theory is tested on: THE PRESENT TREATMENT CONCERNS THE SIMPLEST DECISION TASK IN WHICH A PERSON CHOOSES BETWEEN TWO AVAILABLE PROSPECTS
span.quote: Finally, it should be noted that the present treatment concerns the simplest decision task in which a person chooses between two available prospects.

span.label: How compound or many-outcome prospects are reduced to simple ones has not been investigated.
span.note: what this limits: any application to compound prospects: THE MANNER IN WHICH COMPLEX OPTIONS, E.G., COMPOUND PROSPECTS, ARE REDUCED TO SIMPLER ONES IS YET TO BE INVESTIGATED
span.quote: The manner in which complex options, e.g., compound prospects, are reduced to simpler ones is yet to be investigated.

span.label: The critique is aimed at one of the criticised theory's two stated uses, not at both.
span.note: what this limits: any claim that this paper refutes expected utility theory: the authors state it is accepted as a normative model of rational choice and separately applied as a descriptive model of economic behavior, and the critique is of the descriptive use
span.quote: It has been generally accepted as a normative model of rational choice [24], and widely applied as a descriptive model of economic behavior, e.g. [15, 4]. Thus, it is assumed that all reasonable people would wish to obey the axioms of the theory [47, 36], and that most people actually do, most of the time

span.label: The proposed theory is stated by its own authors to have normatively unacceptable consequences.
span.note: what this limits: any normative or prescriptive use of prospect theory: the authors state that its departures from expected utility theory must lead to normatively unacceptable consequences
span.quote: The equations of prospect theory retain the general bilinear form that underlies expected utility theory. However, in order to accomodate the effects described in the first part of the paper, we are compelled to assume that values are attached to changes rather than to final states, and that decision weights do not coincide with stated probabilities. These departures from expected utility theory must lead to normatively unacceptable consequences

span.label: The demonstrations rest on a named academic sample and one national currency.
span.note: what this limits: any generalisation of these effects to a population: the demonstrations are based on the responses of students and university faculty to hypothetical choice problems, with outcomes denominated in Israeli currency
span.quote: The demonstrations are based on the responses of students and university faculty to hypothetical choice problems. The respondents were presented with problems of the type illustrated below. Which of the following would you prefer? A: 50% chance to win 1,000, B: 450 for sure. 50% chance to win nothing; The outcomes refer to Israeli currency

However, in order to accomodate the effects described in the first part of the paper, we are compelled to assume that values are attached to changes rather than to final states, and that decision weights do not coincide with stated probabilities. These departures from expected utility theory must lead to normatively unacceptable consequences

Thus, it is assumed that all reasonable people would wish to obey the axioms of the theory [47, 36], and that most people actually do, most of the time

However, in order to accomodate the effects described in the first part of the paper, we are compelled to assume that values are attached to changes rather than to final states, and that decision weights do not coincide with stated probabilities. These departures from expected utility theory must lead to normatively unacceptable consequences

span.label: stated probabilities
span.quote: The equations of prospect theory retain the general bilinear form that underlies expected utility theory. However, in order to accomodate the effects described in the first part of the paper, we are compelled to assume that values are attached to changes rather than to final states, and that decision weights do not coincide with stated probabilities. These departures from expected utility theory must lead to normatively unacceptable consequences

span.label: carriers of value
span.quote: The apparent neglect of a bonus that was common to both options in Problems 11 and 12 implies that the carriers of value or utility are changes of wealth, rather than final asset positions that include current wealth

span.label: expected utility theory - TWO USES UNDER ONE NAME, NAMED IN ONE SENTENCE: accepted as a NORMATIVE model of rational choice - what reasonable people would WISH to do - and applied as a DESCRIPTIVE model of economic behavior - what most people ACTUALLY DO; the paper's critique is of the second use only, and the distinction is carried by those two verbs
span.quote: It has been generally accepted as a normative model of rational choice [24], and widely applied as a descriptive model of economic behavior, e.g. [15, 4]. Thus, it is assumed that all reasonable people would wish to obey the axioms of the theory [47, 36], and that most people actually do, most of the time

span.label: prospect theory - DESCRIPTIVE, AND SAID BY ITS AUTHORS TO FAIL AS A NORM: it keeps the bilinear form of expected utility theory but attaches values to changes and lets decision weights depart from stated probabilities, and the authors state these departures must lead to normatively unacceptable consequences
span.quote: The equations of prospect theory retain the general bilinear form that underlies expected utility theory. However, in order to accomodate the effects described in the first part of the paper, we are compelled to assume that values are attached to changes rather than to final states, and that decision weights do not coincide with stated probabilities. These departures from expected utility theory must lead to normatively unacceptable consequences

span.label: the carriers of value - CHANGES OF WEALTH, NOT FINAL ASSET POSITIONS: the cornerstone of the theory is that value attaches to changes rather than to states that include current wealth, so every quantity in the model is defined relative to a reference point that the model itself does not fix
span.quote: The apparent neglect of a bonus that was common to both options in Problems 11 and 12 implies that the carriers of value or utility are changes of wealth, rather than final asset positions that include current wealth

span.label: contradicts → expected utility theory as a descriptive model
span.quote: Choices among risky prospects exhibit several pervasive effects that are inconsistent with the basic tenets of utility theory.

span.label: contradicts → expected utility theory as a descriptive model of choice
span.quote: In the light of these observations we argue that utility theory, as it is commonly interpreted and applied, is not an adequate descriptive model and we propose an alternative account of choice under risk.

span.label: builds-on → Markowitz [29]
span.quote: Markowitz [29] was the first to propose that utility be defined on gains and losses rather than on final asset positions, an assumption which has been implicitly accepted in most experimental measurements of utility (see, e.g., [7, 32]).

span.label: extends → Markowitz [29]
span.quote: His treatment, however, retains the expectation principle; hence it cannot account for the many violations of this principle; see, e.g., Table I.

span.label: replicates → Allais [2]
span.quote: This pattern of preferences violates expected utility theory in the manner originally described by Allais.

span.label: value function (prospect theory)
span.quote: The value function is normally concave for gains, commonly convex for losses, and is generally steeper for losses than for gains

span.quote: N =72 [83]* [17] The data show that 82 per cent of the subjects chose B in Problem 1, and 83 per cent of the subjects chose C in Problem 2.

span.quote: Each of these preferences is significant at the .01 level, as denoted by the asterisk.

span.quote: When the prospects are reduced, however, the difference in variance between (3,000,.25) and (4,000,.20) may be insufficient to overcome the difference in expected value.
